IXSH-FD: integrated XGBoost-SHAP hybrid framework
for SNP feature discovery
Raid Alzubi · Hadeel Alzoubi
© The Author(s) 2026
Abstract
Background Crohn's disease (CD) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by transmural inflammation, that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the small intestine and colon. The incidence is increasing worldwide, with onset often occurring in early adulthood. The precise cause of this disease remains unclear; however, it is believed to be the result of a complex interaction of immune, genetic, microbial, and environmental factors. Results This study presents a hybrid feature selection framework (IXSH-FD) that integrates multiple statistical methods with the XGBoost algorithm to identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with CD risk. Genotype data were obtained from the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (WTCCC) for CD patients and control groups from the UK National Blood Service and the 1958 British Birth Cohort. In the initial filtering stage, Chi-square and mutual information methods were applied to reduce dimensionality and remove irrelevant SNPs. The selected features were then ranked using the XGBoost embedded technique, with different ranking criteria, and only SNPs that appeared in all folds were considered informative features. Experimental results show that the proposed model achieved a high predictive performance (AUC = 90.81%) and effectively addressed the high dimensionality of the SNP data, identifying a final set of 15 SNPs associated with CD. Conclusions Overall, the hybrid XGBoost-based feature selection framework offers an efficient and interpretable approach for genomic-based prediction of CD risk.
Keywords SNP · Crohn's disease · Feature selection · XGBoost
Introduction
The whole human genome encompasses the entire set of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequences in humans, consisting of approximately three billion base pairs. While human genomes are largely similar, each individual possesses at least three million unique nucleotide variations. Among these variations, single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are the most common type of genetic alteration. Research has identified SNPs as key markers in both rare and complex diseases [1]. While most SNPs occur naturally without functional consequences, some


play a significant role in influencing specific phenotypic traits, such as height, disease susceptibility, resistance to infections, skin color, and responses to medical treatments.
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have successfully identified various SNPs correlated with complex traits [2]. These discoveries have enhanced our perception of the underlying biological processes and hold the potential to improve phenotypic prediction. In the near future, such advancements may contribute to better management of human health. However, since these variants typically account for only a portion of genetic variation, phenotypic prediction using GWAS-identified SNPs has shown increasing promise. As a result, there is a growing interest in investigating the combined effects of the most relevant SNPs. While individual SNPs may have a limited impact on phenotypic variance, aggregating a larger set can capture a greater proportion of genetic influence. To achieve this, identifying the most informative subset of SNPs associated with complex diseases requires the use of feature selection methods.
To predict disease progression, it is essential to recognize risk factors in Crohn's Disease (CD) that help guide personalized therapy and avoid possible complications. Crohn's disease is identified as a complex disease caused by many factors that require a risk assessment, including genetic, environmental, clinical, and lifestyle factors that jointly contribute to the appearance, activity, and outcome of CD. Several genetic variants confer a higher risk and result in earlier onset and more intense disease; the total burden of risk alleles is linked with complications and the need for surgery [3]. Even in the absence of traditional risk factors, CD may contribute to increasing the risk of chronic kidney disease, colorectal cancer, and cardiovascular events. This increases the need for employing more efficient risk assessment for CD patients [4–6]. Combining both genetic and machine learning techniques improves early identification of high-risk patients and may reduce complications and healthcare burden. Continued improvement of predictive models is essential for supporting clinical decision-making in CD management. A major challenge arises in prediction models when the number of features surpasses the number of samples, called the curse of dimensionality [7]. In such cases, the huge array of features may include redundant or irrelevant, or affect the predictor negatively, causing a poor performance of the training model. Identifying the most discriminative SNPs, genomic prediction can be enhanced, reduce the model complexity, improve generalization, and avoid the risk of overfitting. The increasing adoption of feature selection techniques in GWAS studies highlights the essential role of dimensionality reduction in genomic research.
What is the most effective feature selection technique to use?
Feature selection is the process of selecting the most discriminative features for building models in tasks such as classification, regression, and clustering. Feature selection primarily contributes to reducing the feature space, thereby enhancing visualization and interpretability. Moreover, results in more compact models with improved generalization capabilities [8]. These advantages make feature selection a valuable research area, particularly in bioinformatics, where it is used to identify key biomarkers that play a crucial role in determining the phenotype of interest [9]. Three primary approaches can be distinguished among feature selection techniques frequently employed in classification: filter techniques, wrapper techniques, and embedding techniques. Furthermore, a fourth categoryhybrid methods-combines several strategies to improve the efficacy of feature selection [10]. These approaches differ in evaluation metrics, computational complexity, capacity to detect redundant features and interactions among features, and whether feature selection is integrated into the learning algorithm or performed separately [11]. Each category has distinct strengths and limitations, making them more suitable for specific applications. Filter methods can generally be classified as univariate or multivariate. Univariate methods evaluate each feature independently, whereas multivariate methods analyze a group of features together. Because of their structural simplicity and execution speed, univariate methods have gained popularity in dealing with high-dimensional data, such as the Chi-Squared test (Chi2) and information gain (IG). However, because univariate techniques evaluate each feature individually, they fail to identify redundant features and capture interactions among them.


As a result, retaining redundant features and overlooking feature interactions can lead to a decline in model prediction performance [12]. On the other hand, multivariate techniques identify relevant features while eliminating the redundant ones without losing information. Some widely used methods include: Minimal-Redundancy-Maximal-Relevance (mRMR), Joint Mutual Information (JIM), and ReliefF. However, it is important to note that these techniques are mainly focused on pairwise feature interactions. Moreover, while multivariate methods offer advantages over univariate approaches, they are computationally more expensive and do not account for interactions with the classifier. Wrapper methods use the predictive criteria of a selected classification model to guide the process of identifying the optimal subset of features. As the name suggests, the wrapper technique performs feature selection while performing the classification, evaluating the impact of a set of features on model performance. This approach outperforms filter methods in most cases [10]. However, searching through all possible feature combinations is highly computationally expensive. Examples of such methods include particle swarm optimization [13], genetic algorithms (GA) [14], and ant colony optimization [15]. The embedded feature selection method is integrated directly into the classification process. During the training process, the internal parameters of the classifier are adjusted to assign appropriate weights or importance to each feature, optimizing classification accuracy. Consequently, the search for the optimal feature subset and model construction occur simultaneously within a single step [16]. Popular embedded methods include decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, and regularization-based techniques such as elastic net and LASSO. Embedded techniques are considered as a middle ground between filter and wrapper methods, as they incorporate aspects of both techniques [17]. From a computational perspective, embedded methods are generally less intensive than wrapper methods but require more computational resources than filter methods. Certain embedded techniques, such as decision tree-based algorithms, can identify multiple feature interactions [18]. However, their ability to detect interactions becomes less reliable and reduced while increasing the number of features, potentially missing epistatic SNPs with weak individual effects[19]. A possible solution to this issue is to integrate an additional feature selection method within a hybrid model to eliminate redundant features. To gain the advantages of the aforementioned approaches, hybrid techniques employ two or more diverse models. This study proposes a model that integrates two filter methods with an embedded technique, leveraging their respective advantages to improve both accuracy and interpretability. In the first layer, a union of features selected by Chi2 and Mutual Information (MI) methods is constructed to capture complementary information and reduce dimensionality. In the second layer, guided by the success of the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) technique, it was employed as the embedded method to evaluate feature importance, rank SNPs based on their contribution to model prediction, and identify the most informative biomarkers associated with CD.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II provides a review of the related work. Section III details the materials and methods used in this study. Section IV presents and discusses the experimental results. Finally, Section V summarizes the conclusions and outlines possible directions for future research.
Related work
The application of XGBoost in biomedical research has gained significant traction in recent years, demonstrating its effectiveness in various predictive modeling tasks. In [20], XGBoost was utilized to predict the biological activity of molecules based on their molecular structures. The study assessed its performance using seven wellknown datasets, each containing varying numbers of features, with a maximum of 8,500. The results indicated that XGBoost outperformed other machine learning algorithms in predicting biological activity, highlighting its potential in drug discovery and virtual screening. Similarly, in [21], a computational model was developed to predict associations between microRNAs (miRNAs) and diseases using XGBoost. By integrating multiple data sources, including nearly 500 miRNA-disease associations, the model effectively captured complex patterns, leading to accurate predictions of potential miRNA-disease relationships.


XGBoost has also been widely adopted in biomarker identification, with studies demonstrating its superiority over other feature selection methods. In [22], a classifier model was developed to predict and identify specific SNPs as biomarkers for assessing hypertension risk. The study analyzed 19,697 SNPs from 2,052 samples, and XGBoost-based feature selection identified 292 SNPs that outperformed other models. Similarly, [23] introduced a multi-stage feature selection framework for disease detection, employing filter-based methods to reduce the number of features before applying XGBoost to extract the most significant ones. This study, conducted on four clinical datasets with feature counts reaching up to 12,533, demonstrated that the proposed method outperformed several state-of-the-art approaches in identifying key features.
Additional studies have further validated XGBoost's efficiency in feature selection and predictive modeling. In [24], a filter-based feature selection model was used to select and rank 50% of the 1,168 features in a promoter nucleic acid sequence dataset, which were then processed through XGBoost to identify the optimal subset. The model exhibited superior predictive performance compared to other evaluated methods. Similarly, in [25], researchers analyzed SNPs in a specific enzyme contributing to interindividual variability in drug reactions and efficacy. They explored various SNP feature sets for predictive modeling, demonstrating that XGBoost was among the most effective techniques for biomarker data analysis. The study involved multiple sample sets, with a maximum of 2,400 SNPs. In [26], the authors proposed an additive model incorporating prior knowledge of gene structure and introducing constraints to the XGBoost mechanism. Their approach assumed that interactions between SNPs should be restricted to the same gene if no interaction existed between two genes. The model was implemented on a dataset consisting of approximately 4,000 samples and 385 SNPs that met specific conditions. This study further reinforced XGBoost's adaptability and robustness in handling complex biological data. These studies highlight XGBoost's expanding role as a powerful tool in feature selection, disease detection, and biomarker identification, showcasing its strong predictive performance across various biomedical applications. However, researchers often limit the number of features used, avoiding the full feature set by implementing initial filtering, increasing the p-value threshold, or leveraging prior knowledge to reduce the number of features. The integration of XGBoost with hybrid feature selection techniques has become a powerful approach for identifying informative SNPs in high-dimensional genetic datasets. These methods address the challenge of large feature spaces and small sample sizes, improving disease prediction and biomarker discovery in genomics. Hybrid methods typically combine XGBoost's embedded feature importance with filter (e.g., ANOVA, MI) and wrapper (e.g., genetic algorithms, SVM-RFE) techniques. This fusion leverages the strengths of each method: filters quickly reduce dimensionality, wrappers optimize feature subsets, and XGBoost provides robust, scalable ranking of SNPs [22, 27, 28]. Studies consistently show that hybrid XGBoost-based feature selection outperforms single-method approaches in disease prediction tasks. For example, XGBoost-based models achieved high performance compared to genetic algorithms, PCA, and other machine learning classifiers [22, 28, 29]. These methods efficiently identify a small, relevant subset of SNPs, improving both computational efficiency and predictive power. While hybrid XGBoost approaches are effective, challenges remain in handling extreme class imbalance, optimizing hyperparameters, and ensuring the interpretability of selected SNPs. While previous studies have explored XGBoost-based feature selection for genomic data, most employ individual filtering or ranking techniques and primarily focus on predictive performance. The proposed IXSH-FD framework extends these approaches by integrating complementary statistical filtering (Chi2 and MI), modelbased XGBoost feature ranking, and SHAP-based explainability within a unified feature selection pipeline. Unlike conventional workflows that rely on a single criterion, IXSH-FD progressively refines the feature space by combining statistical relevance, model-derived importance, and interpretable feature attribution to identify a compact and potentially biologically relevant subset of SNPs. Furthermore, the framework employs a leakage-free evaluation strategy in which feature selection, hyperparameter optimization, feature ranking, and SHAP analysis are performed exclusively within the training folds of the cross-validation process, ensuring an unbiased assessment


of predictive performance. This integrated methodology enables efficient analysis of high-dimensional GWAS data while improving the robustness, interpretability, and reliability of the selected genetic markers.
Materials and methods
Genotype datasets
To conduct this study, all genotype datasets were obtained from the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (WTCCC) [30]. The CD dataset included nearly 2000 CD cases [31]. Control datasets consisted of the UK National Blood Service Control Group (NBS) [32] and the 1958 British Birth Cohort (58 C) [33], each containing approximately 1500 samples. The genotype data were generated using the Affymetrix 500 K chip, comprising 500,568 SNPs. The WTCCC datasets are subject to controlled access and are available upon approved request through the European Genome-Phenome Archive (EGA). Approval for accessing and using all WTCCC datasets was obtained under reference number 24083. Additional dataset access information is provided in the Data Availability section. Initial filtering of the dataset was performed following WTCCC recommendations; 257 samples and 30,956 SNPs were removed due to poor quality, poor clustering, or deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium [30]. Furthermore, SNPs were filtered using the following thresholds: pp-value < 1 × 10−3, Minor Allele Frequency (MAF) of 1%, and missing rate of 5% [34–38]. After quality control, the final dataset contained 469,612 SNPs. To mitigate potential bias caused by class imbalance, an equal number of case and control samples were selected. After filtering, the final dataset consisted of 1,774 CD cases and 1,774 control samples, resulting in a total of 3,548 samples. The entire dataset was evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. In each fold, approximately 80% of the data were used for training and feature selection, while the remaining 20% were reserved for independent testing. This strategy ensured that every sample served as test data exactly once, providing a more robust and reliable assessment of the proposed framework as presented in Fig. 1.
Mutations can occur in the gene copies inherited from both male and female parents. For each SNP, there are two possible alleles: the major allele, denoted as A, and the minor allele, denoted as B. Each SNP may be either homozygous or heterozygous. Homozygous SNPs occur when both alleles are the same-either AA (major allele) or BB (minor allele)-while heterozygous SNPs contain one major and one minor allele, represented as AB. In this study, an additive genetic model is employed to encode SNPs based on the count of minor alleles present. Under this model, each SNP is assigned a numerical value: 0 for AA (no minor alleles), 1 for AB (one minor allele), and 2 for BB (two minor alleles). This encoding allows for a straightforward representation of genetic variation. Consequently, each individual in the dataset is represented by a numerical feature vector, where each element corresponds to a specific SNP and reflects the number of minor alleles observed. This transformation facilitates the use of SNP data in computational analyses. Consider a dataset containing nn individual samples and qq SNPs. This dataset can be organized into a matrix GG of dimensions nn n nn, where each element GGiiii represents the number of minor alleles observed for SNP jj in sample , as presented in Fig. 2
Fig. 1 General framework of the proposed XSH-FD approach for CD


Additionally, each sample is associated with a binary disease status, denoted by a variable YY ii, where = 1,....,nn . The label YY ii indicates whether the individual is affected by the disease or not. Specifically, a value of YY ii= 1 signifies a case an affected individual, while YY ii= 0 indicates control (healthy individual).
Feature selection
Feature selection plays a pivotal role in reducing dimensionality, improving model interpretability, and enhancing predictive accuracy in complex datasets. The hybrid framework integrates filter and embedded feature selection techniques to balance efficiency and interpretability. Initially, the Chi2 and MI methods are applied to extract complementary and relevant SNPs while minimizing redundancy. Subsequently, the XGBoost algorithm serves as the embedded stage to assess feature significance, rank variants according to their predictive contribution, and highlight key biomarkers linked to CD.
Chi2
The Chi2 test is a simple and widely used filter-based method that evaluates the dependence between categorical features and target variables [39]. Its strengths lie in computational efficiency and interpretability; however, it assumes feature independence and is limited to categorical data, making it less effective for continuous or highly correlated features. Chi2 equation is presented in Eq. 1.
χχ2 = ∑ (OOii − EEii)2

Mutual information
MI measures the amount of shared information between features and the target variable, capturing both linear and non-linear dependencies [40]. MI provides greater flexibility than Chi2 but may overestimate importance in the presence of redundant or correlated features and requires sufficient data to estimate probability distributions accurately. MI equation is presented in Eq.2.

● pppppp ppp is the joint probability distribution of XX and YY, ● pppppp and pppppp are the marginal probability distributions of XX and YY, respectively, ● and the logarithm is typically taken in base 2 (for bits) or base ee (for nats).
Extreme gradient boosting(XGBoost)
Gradient boosting is a machine learning technique that enhances predictive performance by combining multiple weak learners into a strong model. It operates by sequentially training decision trees, with each new tree aiming to correct the errors of the preceding ones. The algorithm employs a loss function to measure the discrepancy between predicted and actual values and updates the model by minimizing this loss through gradient descent [41]. By iteratively refining the model, the algorithm progressively enhances its accuracy until the desired performance level is attained.
XGBoost is an optimized implementation of the gradient boosting algorithm that incorporates a more regularized model framework to mitigate overfitting and enhance generalization performance. It includes a built-in feature importance ranking, which helps identify the most relevant features. The algorithm determines each feature's contribution by analyzing how frequently it is used to split the data across all trees in the ensemble. This ranking can be leveraged to select a subset of the most significant features for model training by applying a threshold to the importance scores and retaining only those that exceed it.
XGBoost ranking criteria
In XGBoost, feature ranking criteria are employed to assess the role of each feature in the model's predictive performance. During the construction of decision trees, XGBoost evaluates potential splits using an objective function that minimizes prediction error. The ranking criteria then aggregate these contributions across all trees to determine overall feature importance. XGBoost provides multiple feature ranking criteria-including information gain, cover, frequency, and SHAP values-each offering distinct advantages and limitations for genomic data analysis.
Information gain quantifies the reduction in entropy achieved by a split, thereby favoring features that most effectively separate classes. It is widely employed for preliminary SNP or gene ranking, although it may overestimate the importance of correlated or frequently split features. Conversely, cover represents the number of samples influenced by splits on a given feature, emphasizing those affecting a larger proportion of the dataset; however, it is less commonly applied in genomics research. Frequency measures how often a feature is used in tree splits-a computationally simple metric that may nonetheless overemphasize features involved in numerous or shallow splits. Collectively, these three metrics-information gain, cover, and frequency-are computationally efficient for large-scale initial screening but may be susceptible to bias arising from feature correlation or tree structure, occasionally failing to distinguish biologically relevant features from noise [22, 28, 42]. In contrast, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values are model-agnostic and quantify each feature's contribution to individual predictions. They provide both local (instance-level) and global interpretability, making them particularly valuable for identifying biologically meaningful SNPs or genes. Due to their ability to capture complex, non-linear interactions and to offer transparent explanations, SHAP values have become increasingly preferred for genomic feature selection and the extraction of biologically interpretable insights [43–46].
Together, the filter methods Chi2 and MI and the embedded XGBoost technique form a complementary framework that efficiently screens features and captures complex non-linear relationships within high-dimensional genomic data.


Method
In this study, the IXSH-FD framework predicts the risk of CD using SNP data. The proposed model has been developed to identify an optimal subset of features related to the disease of interest. A nested five-fold crossvalidation strategy was employed to evaluate the proposed framework and ensure a reliable estimation of its predictive performance. In the outer cross-validation stage, the dataset was divided into five stratified folds while maintaining the case-control ratio in each fold. Each outer iteration used four folds for model development and one fold for independent evaluation. Within the training portion of each outer fold, an inner five-fold cross-validation procedure was applied for feature selection. Specifically, the inner loop employed the embedded XGBoost-based feature selection approach to identify and rank the most informative SNPs using only the available training data, as illustrated in Fig. 3. This nested design prevents information leakage between feature selection and model evaluation, while providing a robust assessment of the proposed model's generalization ability. The final performance metrics were reported as the average values across the five outer folds. To efficiently assess feature-target dependencies, the Chi2 method was employed because of its simplicity and low computational cost. Within each training fold, Chi2 was applied to rank the features, and the top 50,000 features were selected. In parallel, MI was used to identify statistical dependencies, including nonlinear relationships, between the features and the target variable, and the top 50,000 features were retained. The features selected by the two methods were then combined to form a fold-specific union set. This complementary screening strategy substantially reduced the original high-dimensional feature space while retaining features identified as informative by at least one of the two filter methods. The resulting fold-specific union set was subsequently passed to the second stage of the feature-selection framework, where XGBoost-based ranking was performed to further refine the feature space.
In XGBoost, feature importance measures were used to assess the contribution of each feature to the model's predictive performance. Four complementary ranking criteria-information gain (Gain), cover, weight, and SHAP values-were employed to evaluate feature importance from different perspectives. During the inner five-fold cross-validation process, the candidate feature set was independently ranked according to each criterion in each fold, and the top-KK features were selected. For each criterion, only features that were consistently selected across all five folds were retained, resulting in a criterion-specific stable feature set. Following this process, two complementary feature subsets were constructed across the four ranking criteria: an intersection set containing features common to all four criteria and a union set containing features selected by at least one criterion. Different values of KK were evaluated during the feature-selection process, and the optimal threshold was determined based on the resulting model performance.
Fig. 3 Nested cross-validation feature selection workflow


To evaluate the discriminative capability of the selected features and the robustness of the proposed hybrid feature selection framework, six diverse classification algorithms were employed: XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbors, Logistic Regression, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The first five models represent conventional machine learning approaches, while the MLP was included as a deep learning-based classifier to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the selected SNP subsets. By leveraging distinct modeling principles, these classifiers provide complementary assessments of feature relevance and predictive performance, thereby offering an overall evaluation of the selected set of features.
Results
Several experiments were conducted to assess the performance of the proposed feature selection model using accuracy (Eq. 3), recall (Eq. 4), precision (Eq. 5), and AUC. These metrics were computed based on the number of true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN), and true negatives (TN), defined as follows: TP represents the number of samples correctly identified as having CD, FP denotes samples incorrectly classified as having CD, FN refers to samples mistakenly classified as healthy, and TN corresponds to samples correctly identified as healthy. The performance evaluation was conducted following the nested five-fold cross-validation framework described previously. To ensure the robustness and stability of the obtained results, the complete evaluation process was repeated three times using different random seeds while preserving the case-control ratio. The reported classification performance represents the average results obtained from all outer-fold evaluations across the three independent repetitions.

The initial feature reduction step employed Chi2 and MI as preliminary filtering methods to reduce the highdimensional SNP space before the XGBoost-based feature ranking stage. Within each cross-validation fold, the top 50,000 SNPs were independently selected using each method, and their union was used to construct the candidate feature set for subsequent XGBoost ranking. This complementary filtering strategy reduced the dimensionality of the feature space while retaining potentially informative SNPs identified by either method.
Using the resulting candidate SNP sets, XGBoost-based feature ranking was performed using four importance criteria: Gain, Cover, Weight, and SHAP values. Different Top-KK values (Top-500, Top-1000, and Top-2000) were evaluated, with the corresponding number of top-ranked SNPs selected within each fold. As shown in Fig. 4, Top1000 yielded the best overall predictive performance, providing a balance between retaining informative genetic variants and excluding less relevant features. Therefore, Top-1000 was selected as the optimal feature-selection threshold for the subsequent analyses.
Table 1 presents the performance metrics of different feature selection approaches, including Chi2, MI, their union, and XGBoost-based feature rankings (Gain, Cover, Weight, SHAP), as well as the intersection and union of XGBoost rankings. The reported results represent the mean ± standard deviation across 15 outer-fold evaluations obtained from three repetitions of five-fold cross-validation, with a different random seed used for each repetition. Both chi2 and MI selected 50,000 features, effectively removing irrelevant features. MI outperformed chi2 in terms of accuracy (0.7709 vs. 0.7524), precision (0.7859 vs. 0.7678), recall (0.7160 vs. 0.7139), and AUC (0.8580 vs. 0.8363). Combining chi2 and MI features (94,101.2 features) further improved all performance


metrics compared to the individual filters, confirming that integrating complementary features enhances model performance. This improvement is reflected in the increase in all performance indicators. XGBoost-based feature selection produced substantial improvements across all metrics compared to filterbased methods, while drastically reducing the number of selected features. The SHAP-based ranking achieved the highest precision 0.8520 and AUC 0.9233, demonstrating strong discriminative power with an average of only 31.8 selected SNPs. The union of XGBoost features achieved the highest accuracy 0.8345 and recall 0.8043, with an average of 37.2 selected SNPs, indicating that combining features identified by multiple ranking criteria provides strong predictive performance. Notably, the intersection of top features across all XGBoost criteria identified a highly compact set of only 18.2 SNPs on average, while maintaining competitive performance, with an accuracy of 0.8213, precision of 0.8322, recall of 0.7975, and AUC of 0.9052. The strong performance achieved with substantially fewer features makes the intersection particularly promising for subsequent analysis. To further evaluate the robustness and reproducibility of the selected SNP subsets, feature-selection stability was assessed across the five cross-validation folds using three complementary measures: the pairwise Jaccard index, overlap ratio, and Nogueira's stability index. The Jaccard index quantifies the similarity between selected SNP subsets across different folds, whereas the overlap ratio measures the proportion of shared SNPs relative to the smaller selected subset. Nogueira's stability index provides a normalized measure of feature-selection consistency while accounting for the size of the candidate feature space. As shown in Table 2, the Gain-based ranking

strategy demonstrated the highest stability, with a mean Jaccard index of 0.3765 ± 0.0438, an overlap ratio of 0.6330 ± 0.0571, and a Nogueira stability index of 0.6267. Cover and Weight showed comparable levels of stability, with Nogueira indices of 0.6134 and 0.6096, respectively, whereas SHAP exhibited slightly lower stability (0.5839 ). These results indicate that the selected SNP subsets exhibited moderate and consistent stability across different data partitions, with Gain providing the most reproducible feature selection among the evaluated ranking criteria. Furthermore, 15 SNPs were consistently selected across all five cross-validation folds and by all four ranking criteria (Gain, Cover, Weight, and SHAP), suggesting the presence of a highly stable core subset of candidate biomarkers.
Table 3 summarizes the optimal hyperparameters obtained for the XGBoost classifier using RandomizedSearchCV. Hyperparameter optimization was performed by randomly sampling 50 configurations from a predefined search space, including tree complexity parameters (max depth and n estimators), learning parameters (learning rate), sampling parameters (subsample and colsample bytree), and regularization parameters (gamma, reg alpha, and reg lambda). Each configuration was evaluated using 3-fold cross-validation on the training data, with ROC-AUC used as the optimization criterion. A fixed random seed (42) was used to ensure reproducibility. The optimal hyperparameter configuration achieved the highest cross-validation ROC-AUC during the optimization process and was subsequently used for the final model evaluation.
Following the feature-selection procedure described above, the stability of the selected SNPs was further assessed using repeated nested cross-validation. The analysis was performed over three independent repeats of five-fold cross-validation, resulting in 15 fold-level feature-selection evaluations. The consistency of SNP selection was quantified using the pairwise Jaccard index and overlap rate across folds within each repeat. Overall, the three repeats yielded a mean Jaccard index of 0.6260 ± 0.0039 and an overlap rate of 0.8286 ± 0.0195, indicating a consistent feature-selection pattern across different data partitions. The selection patterns and frequencies of the top 30 SNPs across the 15 fold-level evaluations are illustrated in Fig. 5. Fifteen SNPs exhibited a selection frequency of 100% and were therefore retained as the final stable SNP set. To examine the predictive utility of this compact subset, final classification models were constructed using XGBoost, Random Forest, SVM, Logistic Regression, KNN, and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network. The models were fitted using the complete dataset, and the resulting performance is reported in Table 4.
Among the evaluated classifiers, XGBoost achieved the highest overall performance, with an accuracy of 0.8119, precision of 0.8220, recall of 0.7871, and AUC of 0.9081. The MLP neural network also showed competitive performance, achieving an accuracy of 0.7908 and an AUC of 0.8731, while SVM achieved an accuracy of 0.7815 and an AUC of 0.8586. Random Forest obtained an accuracy of 0.7787 and a recall of 0.7631. KNN and Logistic Regression showed lower predictive performance, with AUC values of 0.7789 and 0.7564, respectively. Overall, the results suggest that the 15 stable SNPs retain substantial predictive information despite the considerable reduction in dimensionality and provide useful discriminatory information across different classification algorithms. Table 5 presents a comparative analysis of the proposed IXSH-FD prediction system with previously reported approaches evaluated on the WTCCC dataset for CD classification. The proposed IXSH-FD model achieved an AUC of 0.908, demonstrating competitive predictive performance compared with existing SNP-based

However, these comparisons should be interpreted as contextual rather than direct head-to-head evaluations, as differences in preprocessing strategies, SNP filtering procedures, feature selection methods, and evaluation protocols across studies may affect the reported outcomes and limit the validity of direct performance comparisons. The SHAP summary plot in Fig. 6 provides an interpretable overview of the relative importance and directionality of the 15 consistently selected SNPs in the predictive model. Several SNPs, including rs157613, rs12078461, rs1933641, rs6816863, and rs17116117, exhibited relatively large SHAP values, indicating substantial contributions to the model's predictions. In particular, rs157613 and rs12078461 showed wide SHAP distributions extending in both positive and negative directions, suggesting that their contribution to the model output varies according to their feature values. Similarly, rs1933641 and rs6816863 demonstrated pronounced SHAP values on both sides of zero, indicating heterogeneous effects on the model prediction. Other SNPs, such as rs1553460, rs2416472, rs13126272, and rs10483456, showed predominantly positive contributions for higher feature values,

whereas lower feature values were generally associated with negative or near-zero SHAP values. Overall, the SHAP analysis highlights rs157613, rs12078461, rs1933641, rs6816863, and rs17116117 as prominent contributors to the model's decision process, providing interpretable evidence for their importance within the selected SNP subset. As shown in Table 6, 14 of the selected 15 SNPs have been previously reported in studies investigating genetic associations related to CD. These variants have been examined in GWAS and candidate-gene studies and have

Fig. 6 SHAP summary plot illustrating the contribution and direction of impact of the 15 selected SNPs on the model output


been associated with CD susceptibility, pathogenesis, or disease-related traits. Notably, SNPs such as rs9839841, rs17116117, rs1553460, and rs11887827 have been reported in multiple independent studies, providing further support for their relevance to CD. The high concordance between the SNPs identified by our framework and previously reported genetic associations suggests that the proposed approach captures biologically relevant diseaseassociated genomic signals. The remaining SNP, rs392457, did not have a previously reported association with CD in the literature reviewed. Therefore, rs392457 is considered a computationally prioritized candidate variant. Its identification highlights the capability of the proposed IXSH-FD framework to prioritize potentially informative genetic markers, while further functional investigations are required to determine its biological relevance and potential contribution to CD susceptibility.
To investigate the potential biological relevance of the final selected SNP subset, genomic annotation and eQTL characterization were performed using publicly available resources including the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) dbSNP database and the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Project. The selected variants were annotated according to their genomic coordinates and associated genes, where available. In addition, GTEx-based eQTL analysis was conducted to investigate potential regulatory effects across different tissues. The genomic annotations, GTEx eQTL associations, tissue information, and gastrointestinal eQTL evidence for the selected SNPs are summarized in Table 7. Significant tissue-specific eQTL associations were identified for several variants, including rs13126272, rs4471699, rs17116117, rs1933641, and rs10483456. Notably, rs4471699 showed eQTL associations in gastrointestinal tissues, including transverse colon, sigmoid colon, and terminal ileum, and was also identified as having gastrointestinal eQTL evidence. In contrast, no significant GTEx eQTL associations were identified for several other selected variants in the available GTEx data. These findings provide additional functional context for the selected SNP subset and highlight potential regulatory associations for a subset of the identified variants.
Although the proposed framework was evaluated using repeated cross-validation to assess its robustness across different data partitions, all evaluations were performed within the available cohort. Therefore, the generalizability of the identified SNPs and the predictive performance of the proposed model to independent populations remains to be established. Future work will focus on validating the proposed approach using independent external

cohorts from different populations and/or studies to further assess the reproducibility, robustness, and generalizability of the identified genomic signals.
Conclusion
This study proposed a hybrid feature selection framework that integrates Chi2 and MI methods with the XGBoost algorithm, guided by multiple ranking criteria, to identify significant SNP biomarkers associated with CD. The framework effectively addressed the high dimensionality inherent in genomic datasets, enabling the selection of the most informative and discriminative features for disease prediction. Remarkably, the proposed model achieved superior predictive performance, with an AUC of 90.81%, using only 15 SNPs, thereby demonstrating both efficiency and robustness. Furthermore, the subset of SNPs identified by our model reinforces its validity, as the majority of the selected variants have been previously reported in the literature as being associated with CD. This concordance with existing studies underscores the reliability and biological relevance of the proposed approach. Overall, the hybrid XGBoost-based feature selection model provides a powerful, interpretable, and scalable framework for analyzing complex genetic data. Future research will focus on validating these biomarkers in larger and more diverse cohorts and extending the framework's application to other multifactorial diseases to further assess its generalizability and clinical potential.
